National Register of Historic Places nomination, Gibb, Daniel, & Co. Warehouse (reference number 97001189), National Park Service.
sources.label: National Register of Historic Places nomination, National Park Service

historical_record.description: The land at the southwest corner of Vallejo and Front Streets — then on the edge of the water, about a block west of the present seawall — appears to have been bought by Daniel Gibb, a commission merchant from Scotland.

A two-storey brick warehouse with a basement, 28 feet high on a lot 40 by 110 feet, was built as one of a matching pair with the building at the northwest corner; the designer and builder are not known. Three bays face Front Street and nine face Vallejo, the openings tall and narrow under relieving arches, with a sandstone main entrance in a Gibbs surround, granite sills, a corbelled cornice and marble street signs set into the brickwork at the corner.

The firm of Daniel Gibb & Co. moved in during the first week of September and used the building as its sales office as well as for storage — the gold-rush pattern, where goods were sold from the same room they were kept in.

A city surveyor recorded it as a Class 1 brick building measuring 45 feet 10 inches by 110 feet, two storeys and a basement, with walls sixteen to twenty inches thick, a tin roof and iron coverings over the front and rear openings.

Gibb's firm ended some time in 1864 after his death and his brother William's, and both warehouses were bought about then by a warehouseman, John Sanborn, whose family held this one until 1969 and still owns the twin across Vallejo Street.

City directories name the building Gibbs' U.S. Bonded Warehouse from at least 1879 to 1886; by 1894 the tenant had renamed it the Vallejo Street Free Warehouse, and in 1901 it was the Vallejo Street Bonded Tea Warehouse.
The fire that followed the earthquake gutted both warehouses and brought down parts of their walls; this one kept more of its 1855 brickwork than its twin.

After the fire, both warehouses were rebuilt on what was left of the original walls to very nearly their earlier appearance. The seam between the two dates of brickwork is still plain — stretchers with smooth pointing below, American bond with rough pointing above — running under the tops of the Front Street second-floor windows, dipping almost to the street signs at the corner, then rising nearly to the cornice along Vallejo. The 1855 brickwork survives for the whole first floor and nearly half the second; the replacement cornice is plainer corbelling and two upper Front Street windows were left out.

A Sanborn map of 1913 records the building in use for wine storage and reverse directories of 1933 and 1940 give it to a seed company. About then the Trinidad Bean and Elevator Co. took it over for sorting, cleaning and storing beans grown in Colorado, and stayed until about 1972; it built or acquired a skylit mezzanine at the west end of the second floor for hand-sorting, and beams in the basement still carry its stencilled labels for lentils and garbanzos.

The building was converted from warehouse to offices. The brick was sandblasted back from paint, the Front Street loading dock removed, a pair of second-floor windows recut on Front Street where they had been before 1906 — without the relieving arches or raised surrounds of the rest — one bricked-up Vallejo window reopened and another turned into a door. A ductile bridge system was built inside for seismic strength without taking out 1855 or 1906 fabric, and the mezzanine was removed.

Listed on the National Register of Historic Places. It and its twin appear to be the oldest warehouses left in San Francisco and the only ones surviving from the gold rush, when storage and selling were still done in the same building.

hook: One of a pair of 1855 warehouses, the oldest in the city, rebuilt on its own walls after 1906.

building.name: Gibb, Daniel, & Co. Warehouse
building.completed_conflict: The assessor's roll gives 1906, the year the warehouse was rebuilt after the fire; it was first built in 1855 and the ground floor and nearly half the second are still that brickwork.
